Latent-driven Imputation and Forecasting for partially observed Time Series (LIFTS) (https://arxiv.org/html/2610.03916v2)
citeturn76view0 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: today; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://arxiv.org/html/2610.03916v2","lineno":90}); Total lines: 1397
L80: ###### keywords
L81: 
L82: Partially observed time series, State-space models, Informative missingness, Imputation, Forecasting, Energy scores
L83: ## 1 Introduction
L84: Partially observed multivariate time series arise in a wide range of scientific and operational settings, including physiological monitoring, wearable sensing, environmental surveillance, financial systems, and brain imaging analysis (【52†Reyna et al., 2020】; 【53†Fortuin et al., 2020】; 【54†Tashiro et al., 2021】; 【55†Li et al., 2024】). Two inferential tasks are particularly important in such applications.
L85: One is retrospective imputation, which aims to recover measurements that were not recorded, and the other is forecasting that characterizes the distribution of future trajectories given the information currently available. Although these tasks are often studied separately, they are closely connected: both require learning the temporal and cross-variable dependence of the underlying process, together with the uncertainty induced by partial observation.
L86: This common structure motivates a unified probabilistic treatment of imputation and forecasting.
L87: Partial observation complicates these tasks, especially when the observation process is informative. Measurements are often not collected according to a fixed design, but their timing and availability may depend on external constraints, operational decisions, resource availability, or the evolving state of the system. The observation process becomes informative when these factors are associated with the underlying trajectory.
L88: This phenomenon is particularly pronounced in clinical settings, where the timing and frequency of laboratory tests, vital signs, and other measurements may depend on the patient’s underlying physiological state (【56†Wells et al., 2013】; 【57†Weiskopf et al., 2013】; 【58†Sisk et al., 2021】). Consequently, the missing mask is more than an indicator of unavailable entries: it is an observed stochastic process that may contain information about the underlying trajectory.
L89: Ignoring this information, or failing to account for its dependence on the underlying process, can mischaracterize the conditional distributions targeted by imputation and forecasting, resulting in biased predictions, miscalibrated uncertainty, and misleading downstream analyses (【59†Little and Rubin, 2019】; 【60†Mitra et al., 2023】).
L90: Existing methods for partially observed time series have largely addressed this challenge by incorporating the observation mask into flexible predictive models.
L91: Sequence-based methods, such as (【61†Che et al., 2018】; 【62†Cao et al., 2018】; 【63†Du et al., 2023】), use recurrent or attention-based architectures to learn temporal and cross-variable structure from observed values and their mask , while generative methods produce distributional imputations by sampling multiple completions conditional on observed data and masks (【53†Fortuin et al., 2020】; 【54†Tashiro et al., 2021】).
L92: Although including the mask can improve prediction, it does not specify how observation patterns are generated or how they relate to unobserved measurements. Conditioning on the mask alone may therefore be insufficient to account for informative observation when estimating the distributions needed for imputation and forecasting.
L93: A separate literature on nonignorable missing data jointly models measurements and their observation indicators, but these methods have been developed primarily for non-temporal multivariate data (【64†Ipsen et al., 2020】; 【65†Ma and Zhang, 2021】; 【66†Xie et al., 2026】; 【67†Liu, 2026】; 【68†Yang et al., 2026】).
L94: A methodological gap therefore remains for a flexible dynamic framework that jointly models complete measurements and observation patterns and provides a coherent basis for probabilistic imputation and forecasting under informative observation.
L95: To address this gap, we adopt a latent-driven approach, in which an evolving latent state jointly governs the complete measurement trajectory and the missingness mask, as illustrated in Figure 【69†1】. The mask is therefore not merely a bookkeeping device, but an additional manifestation of the underlying state that can inform inference and downstream analysis.
L96: Marginally, the shared dependence on the latent state generally induces a missing-not-at-random mechanism, because observation probabilities may depend on unobserved measurements through that state. By linking the observation process to a shared latent state rather than directly to a high-dimensional complete measurement history, the formulation provides a parsimonious and operational way to accommodate complex, time-varying observation patterns without separately specifying a mechanism for each pattern.
L97: It represents a structured class of informative observation mechanisms rather than all possible missing-not-at-random mechanisms (【70†Rubin, 1976】; 【71†Mealli and Rubin, 2015】).
L98: 【72†Image: Refer to caption】 Figure 1: Illustration of the latent-driven view of a partially observed time series. An evolving latent state jointly governs the complete measurement vector and its observation mask.
L99: Building on this formulation, we propose LIFTS (Latent-driven Imputation and Forecasting for partially observed Time Series), a probabilistic framework based on a nonlinear state-space model, where a latent transition governs temporal evolution and two output mechanisms generate the complete measurements and their observation masks.
L100: LIFTS complements this generative model with learned forward-backward inference. In the forward pass, an encoder represents the latent filtering distribution given the history of recorded measurements and masks, providing the starting point for forecasting through the generative model. In the backward pass, a smoother incorporates future information to generate smoothed latent trajectories. An imputation decoder then samples missing measurements conditional on these states and the observed measurements.
L101: The generative and inference components are parameterized by neural networks and trained jointly using sample-based energy-score objectives (【73†Gneiting and Raftery, 2007】; 【74†Székely and Rizzo, 2013】), with randomly withheld observed measurements providing training targets for imputation.
L102: Our theory clarifies why this inference structure is appropriate and when learning from partial observations can recover the full trajectory law. Under the general model, we show that suitable conditional maps reproduce the target forecasting and imputation laws. In particular, the backward recursion recovers the joint smoothing distribution, preserving temporal dependence rather than only reproducing time-wise marginals.
L103: We also establish strict propriety of the masked energy score, ensuring that its population objective targets the joint law of recorded measurements and masks, including their dependence. However, learning this observed-data law does not by itself identify the distribution of unobserved measurements. For an explicit structural subclass, we establish full-law identification and consistency of the corresponding model-based estimator under the stated assumptions.
L104: These results provide sufficient conditions under which learning the observation law can recover the joint distribution of complete measurement trajectories and masks. They complement identification results for generative missing-data models (【65†Ma and Zhang, 2021】; 【66†Xie et al., 2026】) and identification-guided energy-score imputation (【68†Yang et al., 2026】), with the focus here on joint trajectory laws under common latent dynamics and their connection to forward-backward inference.

Robust prediction under missingness shifts (https://arxiv.org/html/2406.16484v1)
citeturn76view2 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: today; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://arxiv.org/html/2406.16484v1","lineno":90}); Total lines: 707
L78: Most approaches follow a two-stage process: find a (good) imputation, and then fit a standard prediction model to the completed data (【59†Wood et al., 2015】; 【60†Le Morvan et al., 2021】). Others bypass imputation and learn separate submodels for each missingness pattern (【61†Fletcher Mercaldo & Blume, 2020】) or optimally embed the missing data for prediction (【62†Le Morvan et al., 2020】).
L79: Which approach is ultimately chosen usually depends on the prediction performance in held-out test data. Performance-based model selection tends to favour models that can also exploit information encoded in the missingness (【58†Perez-Lebel et al., 2022】; 【63†Rockenschaub et al., 2023】; 【64†Sisk et al., 2023】).
L80: Exclusively focusing on prediction performance ignores a key challenge, though: the mechanisms that govern which covariates are observed and which are missing may — and often do — change once a model is deployed in the real world (【65†Sperrin et al., 2020】). For instance, reduced costs can influence how often clinical tests are performed, with the recent increase in MRIs as a prime example (【66†Smith-Bindman et al., 2019】). Clinical guidelines may similarly evolve over time.
L81: In either case, missingness changes and no longer carries the same meaning, potentially invalidating the learned relationships. Even the introduction of the model itself can shift how and when data are collected (【65†Sperrin et al., 2020】).
L82: This immediately raises two critical questions which form the core of this paper: If the mechanisms of missingness change during deployment, can methods that leverage informative missingness still maintain their edge? Is there an advantage in using methods that might be less performant but do not rely on informative missingness? To answer these questions, this paper discusses the theoretical conditions under which predictions remain reliable when missingness changes, and empirically evaluates the robustness of several common prediction methods under those conditions.
L83: In doing so, we make the following contributions:
L84:   * •
L85: 
L86: We formalise the effect of missingness shifts on the optimal predictor from a missing data perspective, showing that even estimators that utilise informative missingness remain valid if missingness is ignorable in both the source and target environment.
L87: 
L88:   * •
L89: 
L90: We demonstrate that although all estimators may theoretically achieve robust predictions under ignorable missingness shifts, they do not always do so reliably.
L91: 
L92:   * •
L93: We introduce NeuMISE, a novel neural architecture that provides competitive prediction performance while remaining comparatively robust in the presence of ignorable shifts.
L94: ## 2 Related work
L95: Learning with missing data 【67†Rubin (1976)】 established conditions for valid inference from partially missing data (see Appendix 【29†C】 for a detailed summary). Without information on the exact mechanisms that influence missingness, they showed that unbiased estimation of the full data distribution is possible if data is Missing (Completely) At Random (M(C)AR) — i.e., if missingness only depends on observed values. Missingness of this types is said to be ignorable (【67†Rubin, 1976】).
L96: If missingness depends on unobserved quantities, however, data is considered Missing Not At Random (MNAR). Additional information not deducible from the data alone is necessary for valid inference (【68†Mohan & Pearl, 2021】). Since this is hard to come by in practice, most approaches for dealing with missing data assume data are M(C)AR, which may often be implausible (【60†Le Morvan et al., 2021】).
L97: Impute-then-regress Since most off-the-shelf prediction models require fully-observed features, missing values are frequently imputed prior to model training. Methods for imputation range from conditional mean imputation to full estimation of the posterior probability of the missing values. The latter is motivated by 【57†Rubin (1987)】, which promises unbiased estimation of the complete data model^{1}^{1} 1 That is, the model that minimises the prediction loss had we had completely observed data.
L98: if done correctly. One of the best known imputation algorithms is Imputation by Chained Equations (ICE), which iteratively trains one conditional imputation model per variable (【69†White et al., 2011】). Increasingly, machine learning is used to generate imputations, either as part of ICE (【70†Van Buuren, 2018】) or directly through the use of generative models such as (variational) autoencoders (【71†Mattei & Frellsen, 2019】) or generative adversarial networks (【72†Yoon et al., 2018】).
L99: Prediction without imputation 【73†Rosenbaum & Rubin (1984)】 first considered fitting a separate submodel per missingness pattern, thus bypassing the need for imputation and allowing the model to utilise information encoded in the missingness pattern. This idea was revisited by 【74†Josse et al. (2020)】, who showed that pattern submodels minimise the empirical loss. 【60†Le Morvan et al.
L100: (2021)】 further proved that any non-probabilistic impute-then-regress approach asymptotically estimates a pattern submodel, provided that a suitably flexible predictor is used. However, the difficulty of estimating a model for all possible missingness patterns — which grow exponentially with the number of covariates — was already noted by 【73†Rosenbaum & Rubin (1984)】.
L101: The potential sparsity of data may be avoided by considering only common patterns (【61†Fletcher Mercaldo & Blume, 2020】) or by allowing patterns to share information (【62†Le Morvan et al., 2020】).
L102: Distribution shift Distribution shifts are an active area of research, with a strong focus on covariate or label shifts (【75†Cai et al., 2023】). Changes in missingness have been relatively understudied and mostly limited to illustrative examples (【76†Groenwold, 2020】) or empirical investigations (【77†Jeanselme et al., 2022】). Only very recently, 【78†Zhou et al.
L103: (2023)】 formally introduced the notion of missingness shifts in the context of domain adaptation, showing that they reduce to covariate shifts if the missingness is ignorable. Here, we expand on this result from a missing data perspective.
L104: ## 3 Problem definition
L105: Covariates Following 【60†Le Morvan et al. (2021)】, we consider $N$ i.i.d. realisations of the random vector $(X,M,Y)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\{0,1\}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}$, where $X$ are the complete (counterfactual) covariates, $M$ are the missingness indicators, and $Y$ is the outcome. For a single $(x,m,y)$ realisation, $m^{(j)}=1$ indicates that $x^{(j)}$ is missing and $m^{(j)}=0$ means that it is observed. The complete covariates $X$ are generally not available in practice.
L106: Instead, we only have access to the partially-observed covariates $\tilde{X}\in(\mathbb{R}\cup\{\texttt{NA}\})^{d}$ denoted as
L107:  | $$\tilde{X}^{(j)}=\begin{cases}X^{(j)}&\text{if }M^{(j)}=0,\\
L108: \texttt{NA}&\text{if }M^{(j)}=1,\end{cases}$$  |  | (1)
L109: where $j\in\{1,...,d\}$ indicates the covariate and NA represents a missing value. We further denote the indices corresponding to observed features by $obs(M)\subseteq\{1,...,d\}$ and missing features by $mis(M)=\{1,...,d\}\setminus obs(M)$. Hence, the observed features are denoted as $X_{obs(M)}$ and missing features as $X_{mis(M)}$. For readability, we use $X_{obs}$ and $X_{mis}$ in the remainder.
L110: 
L111: Outcome Without loss of generality, we assume that the outcome $Y$ is generated according to
